items.stem: In Oracle SQL, which operator concatenates two strings?

options.rationale: Correct: Oracle uses || (or the CONCAT function) for string concatenation.
+ performs arithmetic in Oracle, not string concatenation.
& is a substitution-variable prefix in SQL*Plus, not concatenation.
. qualifies object names; it does not join strings.

items.explanation: Correct: Oracle uses || (or the CONCAT function) for string concatenation.

items.stem: Which TWO are valid reasons to group related PL/SQL procedures into a package?

options.text: To group related logic behind a published specification
options.rationale: Correct: the package spec defines a public interface, hiding body details.

options.text: To allow shared package-level state across calls in a session
options.rationale: Correct: package variables can persist for the duration of a session.

options.text: To bypass all privilege checks on the underlying tables
options.rationale: Packages do not remove privilege requirements.

options.text: To guarantee queries never need indexes
options.rationale: Packaging code has no effect on index needs.

options.text: To convert PL/SQL into plain SQL automatically
options.rationale: A package still contains PL/SQL; it is not translated to SQL.

items.explanation: Correct: the package spec defines a public interface, hiding body details.

items.stem: Why grant privileges through a role rather than directly to each user?

options.text: A role centralises privilege management and can be granted to many users at once
options.rationale: Correct: roles make privileges easier to assign, revoke and audit consistently.
Roles are an access-control construct, not a performance feature.

options.text: Roles remove the need for a password
options.rationale: Authentication is separate from role-based authorization.
Roles have nothing to do with indexing.

items.explanation: Correct: roles make privileges easier to assign, revoke and audit consistently.
